chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Abu Yahya al-Wasiti, raising it (marfu'), said:

The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) passed by the butchers and forbade them from selling seven things from the sheep. He forbade them from selling blood, glands, the two ventricles of the heart, the spleen, the spinal marrow, the testicles, and the penis.

One of the butchers said to him: 'O Commander of the Faithful, is the liver and the spleen not the same?' He said to him: 'You lie, O dimwit! Bring me two containers of water; I shall inform you of the difference between the two.' So they brought a liver, a spleen, and two containers of water.

He (peace be upon him) said: 'Cut the spleen from its middle, and cut the liver from its middle.' Then he (peace be upon him) ordered that both be immersed in the water together. The liver whitened and nothing was lost from it, but the spleen did not whiten — all that was inside it came out and became blood entirely, until only the skin of the spleen and its veins remained. He then said: 'This is the difference between the two: this (liver) is flesh, and this (spleen) is blood.'

key_terms.الطِّحَال: Spleen — prohibited to sell or eat because it is considered essentially blood
key_terms.رَفَعَهُ: Marfu' — a term in hadith sciences indicating the chain is elevated/connected to the Imam without naming all intermediaries
key_terms.لُكَع: A term of rebuke meaning 'dimwit' or 'base person', used colloquially in classical Arabic

ai.seo_question: What parts of a sheep is it forbidden to sell or eat in Islam according to Imam Ali?
ai.summary: Imam Ali (peace be upon him) forbade butchers from selling seven specific parts of a sheep, including blood, glands, spleen, spinal marrow, testicles, and penis — all classified as prohibited (haram) in Islamic jurisprudence. When a butcher challenged the distinction between liver and spleen, the Imam demonstrated empirically by immersing both in water: the liver whitened (flesh), while the spleen dissolved into pure blood, confirming its prohibition. This hadith reflects Imam Ali's authority in both governance and religious law, and his use of observable evidence to settle jurisprudential disputes.
